content:
[reinforce_legal updated="7 October 2026" lede="How Reinforce Lab collects, uses and protects your information when you use our website, forms and store, and the choices you have."]

Who we are

Reinforce Lab Limited (registered in Bangladesh, RJSC registration no. C-180618/2022) is the company responsible for your information (the "data controller"). Our registered office is Suite #1402, Level-13, Concord Tower, 113 Kazi Nazrul Islam Avenue, Dhaka 1000, Bangladesh. We also work from 2511 Pines Pointe Dr, Katy, TX 77493, USA, through our US company, Reinforce Lab Inc.

For anything about privacy, email hello@reinforcelab.com. We have not appointed a data protection officer; your email reaches the people who handle these requests.

What this policy covers

This policy covers our website, our forms, our online store and the emails you send us. When you become a client, the information we handle for you (for example access to your analytics or your website) is covered by our agreement with you.

What we collect

Information you give us

  • Contact form: your name and email address, and, if you choose, your company, website, the topic and your message.
  • Search Authority Diagnostic and SEO & AI Search Audit request form: your name, work email and company, and, if you choose, your website, role, industry, biggest search challenge, monthly content volume and desired outcome.
  • Orders from our store: see "Orders and payments" below.
  • Emails and calls: whatever you choose to tell us when you email or phone us.

Fields marked as required are the minimum we need to reply to you; everything else is optional. Each form tells you, before you send it, why we need your details, how long we keep them, where they are stored and how to withdraw, and asks you to tick a box to agree. We record that you agreed and when. Please do not send us sensitive information, such as health information, through the forms.

Information collected automatically

  • Website analytics: if you agree to analytics cookies, we use Google Analytics to understand how the website is used. See "Cookies" below.
  • Visit statistics: we use Jetpack Stats, a service from Automattic, to count visits and see which pages are read. Your browser connects to Automattic's servers, which receive technical information such as your IP address, browser type and the pages you view. We see totals, not who you are. Jetpack Stats does not set cookies on our pages.
  • Fonts: our fonts are served from our own website, not from Google, so loading a page does not send your information to a font provider.
  • Spam protection: when you send a form, we keep a scrambled (hashed) version of your IP address for one hour to limit repeated submissions. It is then deleted automatically.
  • Server logs: our hosting provider, Hostinger, records technical requests (IP address, date and time, page requested) to keep the website running and secure.

Cookies

Cookies are small files a website stores in your browser. We use two kinds:

CookieWhat it doesWhen it is setHow long it lasts
Google Analytics (_ga, _ga_*)Tells visits apart so we can see how the website is used, in totalsOnly after you accept analytics cookiesUp to 2 years
Your cookie choice (rl_consent, kept in your browser's local storage, not a cookie)Remembers whether you accepted or declined analytics cookies, so we do not ask on every pageWhen you choose6 months, then we ask again
Store and login cookies (WooCommerce, WordPress)Keep your cart and checkout working, and keep our team logged inWhen you use the cart or checkout, or log inFrom the end of your visit up to a few days

When you first visit, we ask whether you accept analytics cookies. If you decline, or your browser sends a Global Privacy Control signal, no analytics cookies are set and the website works the same. You can change your choice at any time with the "Cookie settings" link at the bottom of every page, or by clearing cookies in your browser.

Orders and payments

When you buy from our store, we collect what we need to process and deliver your order: your name, email address, phone number, billing address, the products you buy and your order history. Payments are made through our payment provider: you enter your card or payment details on the provider's secure form, the provider processes the payment, and we do not see or store your full card number. We will name our payment provider on this page before the store opens on this website.

We use order information to complete your order, send receipts and updates, handle refunds and support, and keep the records that tax and accounting laws require.

How we use your information

What we doWhy we are allowed to
Reply to your message or requestYour consent, given with the tick box on the form; you asked us to (steps before a possible contract); and our legitimate interest in answering enquiries
Prepare your Search Authority Diagnostic or audit proposalYour consent, given on the form, and steps you asked us to take before a possible contract
Follow up about your requestOur legitimate interest in following up an enquiry you made; you can tell us to stop at any time
Process and deliver store orders, and handle refundsOur contract with you
Measure how the website is used with Google AnalyticsYour consent, which you can withdraw at any time
Keep the website working, secure and free of spamOur legitimate interest in running a safe website
Count visits in totals with Jetpack StatsOur legitimate interest in improving the website
Keep tax and accounting records for orders and clientsLegal obligation

We do not sell your information. We do not use it for advertising, and we do not add you to a newsletter unless you ask to join one. We do not make decisions about you based only on automated processing.

Who we share it with

We share only what each provider needs to do its job for us:

  • Hostinger, which hosts our website and our email, including the hello@reinforcelab.com mailbox that receives form messages;
  • Google (Google Analytics, only with your consent) and Automattic (Jetpack Stats), as described above;
  • our payment provider, for store orders;
  • professional advisers, such as accountants or lawyers, when needed;
  • authorities, when the law requires it.

International transfers

Reinforce Lab Limited is based in Bangladesh, and our team also works from the United States. When you send us a form or an email, you send your information directly to us. Our service providers may process it in other countries; when they do, we rely on their safeguards, such as the European Commission's standard contractual clauses where they apply, and we transfer information out of Bangladesh only as Bangladesh's data protection law allows.

How long we keep it

  • Form submissions and emails that do not lead to work: up to 24 months, then deleted.
  • Information about clients and store orders: for as long as we work together or the order needs support, then as long as tax and accounting laws require.
  • Google Analytics data: up to 14 months.
  • Spam-protection records: one hour.

How we protect it

The website uses HTTPS. Form submissions are stored as private records that only our team can open, and access is limited to the people who need it. No method of sending or storing information is completely secure, but we work to protect yours and will tell you and the authorities about a serious breach as quickly as the law requires (for example within 72 hours to the authority under the GDPR).

Your rights

Depending on where you live, you can ask us to:

  • tell you what information we hold about you and give you a copy;
  • correct it;
  • delete it;
  • stop or limit how we use it, or object to a use based on our legitimate interests;
  • send it to you or another company in a common format;
  • withdraw consent you gave, at any time, without affecting what we did before.

To make a request, email hello@reinforcelab.com. We will reply within one month and may ask you to confirm who you are.

Depending on where you live

  • European Union and European Economic Area: you have the rights above under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and you can complain to the data protection authority in your country.
  • United Kingdom: you have the same rights under the UK GDPR and can complain to the Information Commissioner's Office.
  • Bangladesh: under the Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025, your personal data belongs to you. We process it with your consent or where the law allows without it, you can withdraw consent at any time and we then stop that processing, and you can ask to see, correct or delete your data.
  • United States: you can ask what we collect and ask us to delete it. We do not sell personal information or share it for targeted advertising. If your browser sends a Global Privacy Control signal, we treat it as a request to opt out and do not load analytics cookies.
  • Elsewhere: we give everyone the rights above, whatever the local law requires.

Children

Our website, store and services are for adults and businesses. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 18, and we never track or profile children or show them targeted advertising. If you think a child has sent us information, email us and we will delete it.

Links to other websites

Our pages link to other websites, such as LinkedIn, Facebook, Instagram, Clutch and the sources we cite. Their own privacy policies apply when you visit them.

Changes to this policy

When we change this policy we update the date at the top of this page. If a change is significant, we will say so here.

Starting the work

After your order, we contact you within 2 business days to start onboarding: access to your website and tools, your goals, and any content we need. The timelines on the package page start once we have what we need from you.

Monthly and yearly packages

You confirm that the content and materials you give us are yours to use and do not break anyone's rights.

Nothing in these terms limits or excludes our responsibility for death or personal injury caused by our negligence, for fraud, or for anything else the law does not allow us to limit.

Law and disputes

These terms, and any order, are governed by the laws of Bangladesh.

If a problem comes up, please email us first; we reply within 5 business days and most issues are solved that way. If we cannot resolve it within 30 days, the dispute will be settled by arbitration under the rules of the Bangladesh International Arbitration Centre (BIAC), held in Dhaka, in English, under the Arbitration Act 2001. title: What Is an AI Growth System?
content:
What does an AI growth system actually do?

It takes work that normally passes by hand between people and tools, and connects it. A typical growth team runs five separate activities. Research finds what buyers ask and what competitors miss. Production makes pages, posts and emails. Visibility covers Google and AI search. Conversion covers enquiries and follow-up. Reporting closes the loop. Each usually has its own tool and its own owner. The work moves between them by copy and paste, meetings and spreadsheets, and the lessons from one step rarely reach the others.

An AI growth system joins those steps so the output of one becomes the input of the next. The questions customers ask in sales calls shape the next brief. The pages that bring in qualified enquiries get refreshed first. The reply to a new lead starts from what the system already knows about the company and the page they read. AI does the reading, sorting, drafting and checking in between; people decide what matters, what is true and what is sent.

What are the four layers?

Every AI growth system we build has the same four layers. What changes from one business to the next is the data, the workflows and what is measured.

  1. Data. Your CRM, website analytics, Google Search Console, content and sales notes. They are connected so each step works from the same facts. This includes signal capture: recording what buyers do so the system can act on their intent. Buyer signals include the searches that bring them in, the pages they read, the forms they fill in and the replies they send. Clean data matters more than lots of data. Without this layer, AI works from guesses.
  2. AI models. Models that research, summarise, sort and draft. They work from clear instructions, your approved sources and your standards. They supply capacity, not judgment.
  3. Workflows. The automated steps between tools, built on platforms such as Make or n8n and on the software you already pay for. This is where lead scoring, routing and follow-up happen. It is also where most manual hours are removed, and where approval points are placed.
  4. Reporting. A dashboard that tracks results the business cares about, not activity counts. Think hours saved, visibility in Google and AI search, qualified pipeline and revenue.
[reinforce_ag_layers]

A worked example: one enquiry, start to finish

Illustrative example, not a client case. A B2B services firm wants more qualified enquiries from search.

  1. Research. The system reads Search Console queries and recent sales-call notes. It finds a question buyers keep asking that no page on the site answers well.
  2. Brief and draft. An AI model writes a brief with the sources to use and the claims to avoid. A writer and a subject expert produce the page. The evidence check flags two claims without a source, and they are fixed before publishing.
  3. Visibility. The page is published with structured data and internal links. The question joins the set the firm tracks in Google and in AI answers.
  4. Enquiry. A visitor reads the page and fills in the form. The workflow records the page and search that brought them in and adds company details. It scores the enquiry against the firm's fit rules, then routes it to the right partner with a drafted reply.
  5. Follow-up. The partner edits and sends the reply. If there is no response, a follow-up is scheduled. If the enquiry is not a fit, a polite decline is drafted for approval.
  6. Learning. The dashboard links the enquiry to the page and the original question. Next month's research starts from which pages produced qualified conversations, not from which got the most visits.

The same loop can run across the whole funnel: from the first search to outreach, onboarding and retention. No step here is new on its own. What makes it a system is the connection. Each step hands its result to the next without anyone retyping it, and the results change what happens next.

How is it different from AI tools, agents, automation or an agency?

Agents, automations and agencies can all work inside an AI growth system. Some systems use several AI agents, each with one narrow job, and a person approves their work. The difference is the connection: shared data, workflows between the parts, and reporting that changes what happens next.

What should it measure?

Measure the outcomes, not the activity. Useful measures are:

  • Hours saved on repeatable work, measured before and after each workflow goes live.
  • Qualified enquiries and pipeline by source page and search, from your CRM.
  • Visibility in Google: clicks and positions in Search Console. In AI answers: whether you are mentioned, cited and described correctly on a fixed set of questions.
  • Speed from enquiry to first reply.
  • Quality: claims checked, pages passing review, errors caught before publishing.

Google reports clicks from its AI features inside the normal Search Console performance data. So visibility in AI Overviews is measured with the same tools as the rest of search.

What does an AI growth system cost?

It depends on scope. Cost grows with the number of workflows, data sources and approval steps, and with how much content the system produces. Regulated fields and multiple markets add more. A single workflow on tools you already use, such as automated enquiry handling, is a small project. A system that researches, produces and monitors content across markets is a large one. Any honest price comes after mapping the current process, which is why it is worth starting with a diagnostic rather than a price list.

What goes wrong, and what must stay human?

The common failures are predictable:

  • Automating a broken process. If the hand-off was badly designed, automation repeats the mistake faster. Fix the process first.
  • No source of truth. If services, prices and claims are not written down and approved, AI fills the gaps with plausible but wrong text.
  • Publishing without review. Google says it rewards helpful, original content, however it is made. But using automation mainly to game rankings breaks its spam rules.
  • No monitoring. Workflows can stop working without warning when a form, field or tool changes. Someone has to watch the logs.
  • Ignoring data rules. Enquiry and customer data is personal data. Under UK and EU data protection law, you need a lawful reason to use it. In health, pharma and finance, claims also carry extra legal weight.

What stays human: the strategy, the priorities, the truth of every claim, what is published or sent to customers, and the relationships. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework asks any team using AI to keep people in charge and accountable.

How does Reinforce Lab use one itself?

We started building our own AI growth system with this website. We followed a structured, data-driven process and wrote down every step and every decision.

  • Data first. We pulled 16 months of Google Search Console data, Google Analytics 4 reports and a Screaming Frog crawl of the old site. That showed what to keep, fix or remove before any page was planned.
  • Demand checked. We use Semrush to see how many people search for a topic before we plan a page for it.
  • Research before writing. We use Exa, an AI search engine, to read the top results for each topic. We list the questions and terms they cover, then write a page that covers them better and in plain words.
  • AI that does the build. Claude Code, the AI coding agent from Anthropic, builds and edits the pages. It connects to our WordPress site, sets the titles and schema in Yoast SEO, and runs our checks.
  • Automatic checks. Every page is tested before it goes live: our writing rules, an 8th-grade reading level, and a 10-point search and AI-search standard. At the time of writing, all 55 published pages pass.
  • Sources checked on the day. Each outside claim links to its source, and each link is opened and read before publishing.
  • People decide. The founder approves every page, every new URL and every change to an existing one. Each decision is logged with the reason.
  • One post at a time. Articles are published singly, never in bulk.

It uses the same four layers: data (Search Console, Analytics, Semrush), AI models (Claude), workflows and checks, and a record of what changed. This is the first stage of our own system, and we extend it step by step. See how we build these systems for clients.

Do you need one? A five-question test

  1. Does the same information get retyped between two or more tools every week?
  2. Do enquiries wait hours or days for a first reply?
  3. Can you say which pages or searches produce qualified pipeline, as well as traffic?
  4. Do lessons from sales calls reach your website and content?
  5. Do you know whether AI tools such as ChatGPT or Google's AI Overviews describe your business correctly?

A yes to question 1 or 2 is a reason to start. So is a no to two or more of questions 3 to 5. Begin with the hand-off that costs the most time or the most revenue. That is your first system.

How do you start?

Pick one goal and one path: for example, from a buyer's question in search to a qualified conversation. Map who does what today, find the weakest hand-off, and build the four layers around that path only. Prove it works and is measured, then extend the same foundation to the next goal. Search Authority OS is one example of a system built this way, for search and content. Building everything at once is the most common reason these projects stall.

rl_fields.rl_answer: Social media connects people, spreads news, supports learning and gives businesses low-cost reach. It also takes time, spreads misinformation, puts privacy at risk and can affect well-being. Whether the pros outweigh the cons depends on how you use it, so set a goal, set limits and review the effect on you.
rl_fields.rl_takeaways:
Main pros: staying connected, finding communities, fast news, free learning, low-cost business reach, customer service, networking and creative outlets.
Main cons: lost time, effects on well-being for some users, misinformation, privacy and security risks, bullying and algorithm control.
Research on social media and mental health is mixed, so watch your own habits and take extra care with children and teenagers.
Check the source, the date and other reports before you share a post.
Review privacy settings once or twice a year and use two-step login.
For business, track enquiries and orders, not only likes, and keep your own website and email list as a backup.
Weigh the pros and cons by scoring each platform for value and harm over a week.

What tools do I need for a local SEO audit? | You can do a good first audit with free tools: Google Business Profile, Search Console, Analytics and PageSpeed Insights. Paid tools such as BrightLocal, Semrush or Moz Local save time with many locations.
What is NAP and why does it matter? | NAP is your business name, address and phone number. Search engines compare it across the web to confirm your business is real, so it should be identical everywhere.
How do I improve my local SEO after an audit? | Fix the high-impact, low-effort items first, such as wrong details, categories and a review request process. Then build service and location pages, grow reviews and earn honest local links, and check again after 30 days.
Do reviews affect local SEO? | Yes. Reviews are part of how Google judges how well known and trusted a business is, and they strongly affect whether a customer picks you. Ask every customer, reply to every review and never buy or write your own.
Is a local SEO audit different from a regular SEO audit? | Yes. A regular audit focuses on the website. A local audit adds your Google Business Profile, citations, reviews, local pack position and local links, which often matter more for searches tied to a place.
Can AI tools show my local business? | Yes, they can draw on your site, profile, reviews and listings. Check what they say about you, fix wrong details at the source and keep your facts consistent. No method guarantees a mention.

title: Robots.txt for SEO: A Complete Guide
excerpt: Robots.txt tells search engines and AI crawlers which parts of your site they may crawl. What it does, what it cannot do, how to write one and how to test it.

seo._yoast_wpseo_title: Robots.txt for SEO: A Complete Guide (2026) | Reinforce Lab
seo._yoast_wpseo_metadesc: Robots.txt tells search engines and AI crawlers which pages they may crawl. Learn what it does, what it cannot do, how to write one and how to test it.

rl_fields.rl_answer: A robots.txt file is a plain text file at the root of your website that tells search engine and AI crawlers which pages and files they may crawl. It manages crawling, not indexing: to keep a page out of Google, use a noindex tag or a password instead.
rl_fields.rl_takeaways:
Robots.txt controls which parts of your site crawlers may open. It lives at the root, such as example.com/robots.txt.
It does not keep a page out of Google. A blocked page can still be indexed if other sites link to it.
Google supports four fields: User-agent, Disallow, Allow and Sitemap. It ignores crawl-delay.
Each subdomain needs its own file, and Google reads only the first 500 kibibytes.
AI crawlers such as OAI-SearchBot and GPTBot follow robots.txt too, so decide on purpose whether to allow them.
Test the file in a private browser window and in the robots.txt report in Search Console after every change.
rl_fields.rl_faqs:
Do I need a robots.txt file? | Not always. Without one, crawlers assume they may crawl the whole site. A small site with no private or duplicate sections can work without it. Most sites still add one to block admin pages and point to the sitemap.
Can robots.txt remove a page from Google? | No. It only stops crawling. Google says a blocked page can still appear in results if other pages link to it. To remove a page, use a noindex tag, a password, or delete the page.
Where should I put my robots.txt file? | At the root of the site it is for, such as https://www.example.com/robots.txt. Crawlers do not look for it in folders. Each subdomain needs its own file.
How long do robots.txt changes take to work? | Google usually keeps a copy of the file for up to 24 hours. So a change can take about a day to be noticed. OpenAI also says its search systems can take about 24 hours to adjust.
What happens if robots.txt returns an error? | If the file is missing (a 404 error), Google treats the site as having no crawl limits. If the server fails (a 5xx error), Google stops crawling the site for the first 12 hours, then uses the last good copy for up to 30 days.
What is the maximum size of a robots.txt file? | Google reads the first 500 kibibytes of the file. Anything after that is ignored. If your file is close to that size, combine rules or move blocked content into one folder.
Should I block AI crawlers in robots.txt? | It depends on your goal. Blocking OAI-SearchBot keeps your site out of ChatGPT search answers. Blocking GPTBot or Google-Extended only limits use of your content for AI training. If you want AI tools to cite you, allow the search crawlers.
Does Google support crawl-delay in robots.txt? | No. Google lists crawl-delay as a field it does not support. Google supports User-agent, Allow, Disallow and Sitemap.
What is the best robots.txt for SEO? | There is no single best file, because the right rules depend on your site. A good robots.txt for SEO is short: it blocks admin areas, internal search and pages that make endless near-copies, leaves everything useful open, and lists your sitemap. Test it after every change.
What does Disallow: / mean in robots.txt? | It tells the crawlers named in that group not to crawl any page on the site. It is useful on a private test site and a serious mistake on a live one. If your live site is missing from Google, check for this line first.
Does robots.txt affect crawl budget? | It can, on very large sites. Google says crawl budget matters mainly for sites with about 1 million pages or more, or about 10,000 pages or more that change daily. On those sites, blocking pages you never want crawled saves effort. Small sites usually do not need to worry about it.

excerpt: A digital marketing strategy is a plan for reaching your goals online. How to build one in seven steps, ten strategies to choose from and how to measure results.

seo._yoast_wpseo_title: Digital Marketing Strategies: Types, Steps | Reinforce Lab
seo._yoast_wpseo_metadesc: A digital marketing strategy is a plan for reaching your goals online. See how to build one in seven steps, plus 10 strategies to choose from.

rl_fields.rl_answer: A digital marketing strategy is a long-term plan for how a business will reach its goals using online channels. It names the audience, the goals, the channels, the budget and owners, the content and the measures. Build one in seven steps, then review it every month.
rl_fields.rl_takeaways:
A strategy is the long-term plan. A campaign is a time-limited push inside it. A tactic is one action inside a campaign.
Every strategy rests on six parts: audience, goals, channels, budget and owners, content, and measures.
Build it in seven steps: describe the customer, set goals with a number and a date, check what you do now, choose a few channels, plan content around buyer questions, set budget and owners, then measure and adjust.
Two or three channels done well beat seven done badly.
Search work takes time: Google says changes can show in hours or take months, and suggests waiting a few weeks before judging.
Track early signals and final results, and review them every month.
rl_fields.rl_faqs:
What is a digital marketing strategy? | A digital marketing strategy is a long-term plan for how a business will reach its goals using online channels. It names the audience, the goals, the channels, the budget, the content and the measures that show whether it works.
What is the difference between a digital marketing strategy and a campaign? | A strategy is the long-term plan and the reason behind it. A campaign is a time-limited push toward one goal inside that plan. For example, the strategy may be to win small clinics through search content, and one campaign may be a six-week workshop promotion.
What are the main types of digital marketing strategies? | The main ones are search engine optimization, content marketing, pay-per-click advertising, social media marketing, email marketing, influencer marketing, affiliate marketing, mobile marketing, video marketing and search optimized for AI and voice. You do not need all of them.
How do I choose the right digital marketing strategy? | Start with your customer, not the channel. Find out where your buyers look for answers, set a goal with a number and a date, and pick two or three channels that fit both. Test, measure and adjust each month.
How much should I spend on digital marketing? | There is no single right figure. Your budget should cover media spend, tools, content production and staff time, and each channel should have an owner and a goal. Start with the channels that fit your buyers and increase spending only on the ones that bring results.
How long does a digital marketing strategy take to work? | It depends on the channel. Paid ads can bring visits quickly. For search, Google says some changes take a few hours and others several months, and suggests waiting a few weeks before judging whether a change helped. Review your numbers every month.
How do I measure whether my strategy works? | Track early signals, such as visits, sign-ups and replies, and final results, such as enquiries, sales and revenue. Use Google Search Console and your analytics tool, set your goals before you start, and compare before and after.
Does SEO still matter with AI search? | Yes. Semrush notes that the same authority and content structure that earn search rankings also shape which sites AI tools cite. Clear answers, clear authorship and consistent facts help in both.
What are the best online marketing strategies? | The best ones are the ones that fit how your customers buy. Search and content suit people who research before buying, email suits repeat customers, and ads suit people who need an answer now. Start with two or three, measure them, and add more only when the first ones work.
What is a good digital marketing strategy for a small business? | Choose one main goal, start with the channels you can run well, such as search content and email, make your website do the selling, ask for reviews and referrals, and keep a simple one-page tracker of your goal and monthly numbers.
What is the difference between online marketing strategies and digital marketing strategies? | In practice there is very little difference. Online marketing, internet marketing and digital marketing all describe plans for reaching customers through the internet and digital tools. Digital marketing is the wider term, because it also covers things such as text messages and app messages.

excerpt: What keyword difficulty is, how tools score it, what a good score is for your site and how to check a keyword step by step, with worked examples.

seo._yoast_wpseo_title: Keyword Difficulty in SEO: Meaning and Use | Reinforce Lab
seo._yoast_wpseo_metadesc: What keyword difficulty is, how tools score it, what a good score is and how to check a keyword step by step, with worked examples. A free plain guide.

rl_fields.rl_answer: Keyword difficulty (KD) is a score, usually 0 to 100, that estimates how hard it is to reach page one of Google for a search term. Tools such as Semrush and Ahrefs calculate it from the strength of the pages that already rank, so scores differ by tool. Use it to compare keywords, then read the real results page to decide.
rl_fields.rl_takeaways:
Keyword difficulty is an estimate made by SEO tools. Google does not publish it.
Scores differ between tools, so compare keywords inside one tool only.
New sites should start with keywords in the 0 to 30 range and move up as links and trust grow.
Always check search intent and the real top 10 results before you choose a keyword.
Counting the links the lower-ranking pages have gives a more useful target than the score alone.
Recheck your target keywords every three to six months.
rl_fields.rl_faqs:
What is keyword difficulty in SEO? | Keyword difficulty is a score, usually from 0 to 100, that estimates how hard it is to rank on the first page of Google for a keyword. Higher means more competition. It is calculated by SEO tools, not by Google.
What is a good keyword difficulty score? | It depends on your site. New sites do best with scores of 0 to 30. Sites with more links and trust can aim for 31 to 60 or higher. Check the keywords you already rank for to find your own reach.
How is keyword difficulty calculated? | Each tool studies the pages that rank in the top 10 and scores how strong they are, often using backlinks, domain and page authority, content quality and search results features. The formulas are private and differ by tool.
Is keyword difficulty accurate? | It is a useful estimate, not a promise. Tools disagree, many lean heavily on links and none know your own site. Use it to make a shortlist and then read the real results.
Is a low keyword difficulty always better? | No. Some easy keywords bring visitors who will never buy. Pick keywords that are winnable and relevant to your business, and check the search intent.
What is the difference between keyword difficulty and search volume? | Search volume is how many times a month people search for a term. Keyword difficulty is how hard it is to rank for it. You need both to choose a keyword.
Can I check keyword difficulty for free? | Yes. Free checkers show a score and volume for a few searches a day. You can also read the top 10 results yourself and use Google Search Console to find phrases you almost rank for.
How do I rank for a high-difficulty keyword? | Build a group of related pages, make the main page clearly better than those that rank, earn links from relevant sites, and expect it to take months. Start with easier related keywords to build trust.
What is long-tail keyword difficulty? | Long-tail keywords are longer, more specific phrases. They usually have lower difficulty and clearer intent, which makes them a good starting point for newer sites.
How often should I recheck keyword difficulty? | Every three to six months, and before you update an older page. Results and scores change as new pages are published and links are earned.

title: Pharma SEO: How Pharmaceutical Companies Get Found
content:
Pharma SEO, also called pharmaceutical SEO or life sciences SEO, is search engine optimization for pharmaceutical and life sciences companies. It helps patients, caregivers, healthcare professionals and business buyers find accurate, approved information about conditions, medicines, research and suppliers. It works inside strict advertising rules, so the plan and the approvals have to be built together.

SEO is one part of pharma digital marketing, which also includes paid search, email, social media and field teams. This guide covers the organic search part. It explains what pharma SEO is, how it differs from ordinary SEO, which rules shape it, and how to run it in eight steps. It includes worked examples, a 90-day plan, questions to ask a pharma SEO company and the mistakes that cost teams the most time. It is not legal advice. Your medical, legal and regulatory team makes the final call on every claim.

What is pharma SEO?

Pharma SEO means making regulated health and company information easy to find in Google and in AI answers, without weakening the evidence or the review process behind it. The mechanics are the same as in any SEO: pages, links, technical health and content that answers real questions. What changes is who owns each page, which statements are allowed and how long a change takes to approve.

It covers four kinds of site:

  • Manufacturer and brand sites. Corporate pages, pipeline pages, product information and disease education.
  • Contract and supply sites. Contract manufacturers, active ingredient suppliers, packaging and testing firms that sell to other companies.
  • Pharmacy and distribution sites. Wholesalers, specialty pharmacies and online pharmacies.
  • Research and education sites. Trial information, medical education and patient groups.

How does pharma SEO differ from general SEO and healthcare SEO?

General SEOHealthcare SEOPharma SEO
Typical siteAny businessClinics, practices, hospitalsManufacturers, suppliers, pharmacies, research bodies
Main audienceCustomersLocal patientsPatients, caregivers, prescribers, business buyers, investors
What you may sayFew limits beyond consumer lawProfessional and advertising rulesTight rules on claims, risk information and who may see product information
Review before publishingEditorClinician or practice ownerOften medical, legal and regulatory review (MLR)
Local searchSometimesCentralRare, except pharmacies
Proof Google looks forHelpful, original contentNamed clinicians, reviewsNamed experts, cited sources, dates, consistent facts

Healthcare SEO helps a practice get found by patients nearby. Pharma SEO is about explaining conditions, treatments, evidence and suppliers to many different audiences, under rules that differ by country and by audience.

Which rules shape pharma search content?

You do not need to be a lawyer to plan SEO, but you do need to know why the review step exists. These are the public sources we checked. Each applies differently to different products and markets, so treat them as background and ask your regulatory team.

SourceWhat it says in plain wordsWhy it matters for SEO
US FDA, draft guidance on online platforms with space limitsIf a firm makes a benefit claim for a prescription drug, it should also give risk information in the same space and a way to reach the full risk information. The FDA notes that guidance documents do not create legal requirements by themselves.A title tag or meta description that states a benefit may need risk information too. Short text does not remove the duty.
US FDA, guidance on presenting risk informationPrescription drug promotion should give a fair balance of benefit and risk information.A product page cannot be built around benefits and leave safety for a link nobody sees.
US FTC, Health Products Compliance GuidanceMarketers are responsible for claims that are stated and for claims reasonably implied. Health claims need strong scientific support.An image, a heading or a comparison table can make a claim. Check the whole page, not only the text.
UK MHRA guidance on advertising medicinesThe ban on advertising prescription-only medicines to the public applies to social networks as well as to traditional media.Public pages about prescription-only medicines need care in the UK. Disease information and product promotion are treated differently.
EU Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88Member States must prohibit advertising prescription-only medicines to the general public.Patient-facing product pages are restricted across the EU. Pages for healthcare professionals follow different rules.
Google, helpful content guidanceGoogle asks for experience, expertise, authority and trust, and holds topics that affect health to the highest standard. It calls these Your Money or Your Life topics.Named authors, reviewers, sources and dates are not extras for pharma pages. They are what Google looks for.

One point sits above the rest. Rules differ by country, by product type and by audience. A page that is fine for healthcare professionals in one market may not be fine for the public in another. Decide the audience and market for every page first.

Who searches, and what do they want?

A pharma site often serves six audiences. Each searches in its own words, so mixing them in one keyword list produces pages that rank for the wrong searches.

AudienceWhat they search (examples)Page that fits
Patientssymptoms of a condition, how a treatment works, side effectsPlain-language disease education, with sources and a review date
Caregiversmanaging a medicine for a parent, what to ask the doctorPractical guides and question lists
Healthcare professionalsmechanism of action, dosing, trial results, prescribing informationEvidence pages, clearly marked as for professionals
Business buyerscontract manufacturer for sterile injectables, active ingredient supplierCapability pages, certifications, case studies, contact forms
Researchers and journaliststrial name, publication, company pipelinePipeline, publications and media pages
Investors and partnerscompany results, partnershipsCorporate and investor pages

What is the difference between branded and unbranded search?

Branded searches include a product or company name. Unbranded searches are about a condition, symptom or treatment class and do not name a brand. They play different roles.

  • Unbranded search builds trust early. A patient who reads a clear explanation of a condition may remember the source.
  • Branded search is mostly navigation. People look for prescribing information, patient resources or contact details.

The link between the two needs care. For prescription medicines, disease education that links straight to product promotion can change how regulators view the education page. Treat internal links on these pages as a compliance question, and ask your regulatory team how the two page types may connect.

How to do pharma SEO: 8 steps

Step 1: Give every search one page owner

List the searches you want to win. For each one, name the single page that should answer it, the audience and the page type. Service pages, guides, glossary entries and product pages can all stay live, but each needs a clear job. If Search Console shows five pages getting impressions for the same phrase, Google cannot tell which one is meant to answer.

Step 2: Map your audiences and markets

Choose the audiences from the table above that matter to your business. Note the country for each. A page for UK patients, a page for EU professionals and a page for US prescribers are three different pages with three different review paths.

Step 3: Build a keyword map by intent

Use a keyword tool and your own Search Console data. Group the searches by audience and by what the searcher wants: to learn, to compare or to contact. Add a column for who must approve the page. Do not target a keyword on a page that cannot say what searchers want to know, for example a price or a claim that is not allowed.

Search (example)AudienceIntentPageReviewer
[condition] symptomsPatientsLearnDisease education pageMedical, regulatory
[drug class] mechanism of actionProfessionalsLearnEvidence page for professionalsMedical, legal, regulatory
contract manufacturer sterile injectablesBusiness buyersCompare, contactCapability pageQuality, legal
[company] clinical trialsResearchersLearnPipeline and trials pageMedical, regulatory

Step 4: Design the page before you write it

Review can remove risk from a page. It cannot give a page a purpose it never had. Before drafting, fix these fields for each page:

  • Audience and market
  • The one question the page answers
  • Claims it will make, and the source for each
  • Approved wording and required safety text
  • Author, reviewer, owner and next review date

Put the answer at the top in two or three plain sentences. Then add detail.

Step 5: Bring SEO into the review process early

Many teams run review first and add SEO after. That turns a small title change into another approval round. Instead, share the keyword map and the page design with medical and regulatory colleagues before drafting, so wording is agreed once. Plan production around real approval times, publish durable pages first and keep a log of approved text that can be reused. Some agencies report approval cycles of several weeks. Check your own, because they vary by company and by content type.

Step 6: Fix the technical basics

  • Crawling and indexing. Make sure public pages can be crawled and indexed. Gate professional-only content clearly, and do not rely on gated pages as landing pages.
  • Speed and mobile. Professionals often search on a phone between appointments.
  • Site structure. Group pages by condition, audience and product, and link them in a logical path.
  • Titles and headings. Use the words your audience uses. Check each title for claims.
  • Structured data. Schema markup tells machines what a page is, such as an article, an organization or a medical web page. Google documents the types it supports. Use markup to describe the page honestly, and do not expect it to lift rankings by itself.
  • Images. Add plain alt text, and check that images do not imply a claim.

Step 7: Show evidence people can check

Authority comes from what a reader can verify. On every page show:

  • The author, with relevant experience
  • The medical or scientific reviewer, with the review date
  • Links to the sources for each important statement, preferring primary sources such as regulators, guidelines and peer-reviewed papers
  • A visible updated date, with changes logged when guidance changes
  • The scope: who the page is for and what it does not cover

Label worked examples as real, anonymized or illustrative. That does not weaken a page. It stops the page from promising evidence it does not have.

Step 8: Measure in stages

StageQuestionWhere to look
DiscoveryAre the right pages indexed and getting impressions?Search Console
OwnershipDoes the intended page get the impressions for its searches?Search Console, by query and page
RankingAre pages moving to positions where clicks happen?Rank tracking
EngagementDo the right visitors read and take the next step?Analytics: scroll, clicks, form fills
QualityAre pages current, sourced and approved?Content log and review dates

Worked example 1: a disease education page

This example is illustrative. A company develops a treatment for a chronic skin condition and wants an unbranded education page for patients in one market.

DecisionChoice
Search"[condition] symptoms" and "what causes [condition]"
Audience and marketAdult patients, one country
Page jobExplain the condition in plain words and say when to see a doctor
Top of pageA three-sentence answer with the author and reviewer named
BodySymptoms, causes, types, when to seek care, questions to ask a doctor
SourcesClinical guidelines and a national health service page, linked
What it avoidsProduct names, benefit claims and links to product pages, unless the regulatory team has approved how the two connect
ReviewMedical and regulatory, with the keyword map shared first
MeasureImpressions and clicks for the condition searches, and time on page

Worked example 2: a contract manufacturer

This example is also illustrative. A contract manufacturer of sterile injectables sells to other companies and has one general "services" page.

  1. Audit. The page is indexed but ranks for nothing, because it lists capabilities in one paragraph.
  2. Keyword map. Four searches: sterile injectable contract manufacturing, fill and finish services, small batch clinical supply, and the company name.
  3. Pages. One capability page for each, with equipment lists, batch sizes, quality certifications the company actually holds, an anonymized project example and a contact form.
  4. Evidence. Named quality head as reviewer, certification numbers and dates, and a changelog.
  5. Measure. Enquiries from organic search tagged by page and tracked into the sales system.

The result is a site that answers a buyer's detailed questions before the first call. Search volume for this kind of term is small, but each visit comes from a qualified buyer.

How do you write titles and descriptions in a regulated field?

Titles and meta descriptions are the first words a searcher reads, and they are short. That makes them easy to get wrong. A few rules keep them safe and useful:

  • Describe the page, do not promote. "Understanding [condition]: symptoms, causes and when to see a doctor" is safer than a line about results.
  • Avoid benefit words for products. Words such as "effective" or "proven" can read as claims. If a product is named, ask what risk information must sit with it.
  • Name the audience. "For healthcare professionals" in a title sets the right expectation and filters out the wrong clicks.
  • Keep them stable. Once approved, a title should not change often, because each change may need review.

How should internal links work?

Internal links tell Google which pages matter and how topics connect. In pharma they also shape how a regulator or reviewer reads a page. Plan them with the same care as the text.

  • Link disease education pages to each other and to related patient resources.
  • Link professional pages to evidence, trial and prescribing resources, not to patient pages.
  • For prescription products, agree with your regulatory team whether and how education pages may point to product pages.
  • Use clear link text that says where the link goes. Avoid "click here".
  • Write the linking rules down, so new pages follow them without a new debate.

How do you handle content for healthcare professionals?

Clinical data pages are valuable for authority, and they carry the highest accuracy risk. Some companies place them behind a professional check. That is a legitimate choice, but it has an SEO cost: search engines cannot read gated pages.

A workable pattern is to keep a public, indexable page that explains what the resource is, who it is for and what it covers, and to gate only the material that requires it. The public page can rank and send the right visitors to the next step. Make sure the public text follows the same approval rules as any other page.

What about pharmacies and distributors?

Pharmacies and distributors often win with local and trust signals more than with long articles. Check these basics:

  • A complete Google Business Profile with the correct name, address, phone number and hours
  • Licence and registration details on the site, in plain view
  • Pages for each service, such as repeat prescriptions or delivery, written in plain language
  • Clear information on what the pharmacy can and cannot advertise about prescription-only medicines in its country
  • Reviews that you ask for fairly and answer without sharing any patient detail

Can pharma companies use AI to write content?

Google has said that using AI is not against its guidelines when the result is helpful and made for people, and that using it mainly to manipulate rankings breaks its spam policies. For pharma the bigger point is accuracy and responsibility. An AI tool can invent a dose, a study or a safety statement that sounds right. Your company is responsible for every claim on its pages.

If you use AI in drafting, keep these rules:

  1. Give it approved source material, not open questions.
  2. Have a qualified person check every fact against the source.
  3. Run the normal medical, legal and regulatory review.
  4. Name the human author and reviewer on the page.
  5. Keep a record of the sources used.

What content types work in pharma SEO?

Content typeAudienceSearch valueReview effort (our judgment)
Disease educationPatients, caregiversHigh: condition searchesMedium: avoid implied promotion
Evidence summariesProfessionalsHigh for medical termsHigh: study data must be exact
Mechanism of action explainersProfessionalsMedium: niche but strong authorityMedium
Capability pagesBusiness buyersHigh for commercial termsMedium: certifications must be current
Glossary entriesEveryoneMedium: short definitionsLow to medium
Pipeline and trial pagesResearchers, investorsMediumHigh
Expert interviewsProfessionalsMedium: builds trustMedium: check disclosures

Pharma SEO and AI search

People now ask AI tools and Google's AI answers about conditions and medicines. These tools summarize pages, and they can get facts wrong. For pharma this is a risk as well as a chance.

  • Put the answer first. A short, direct opening is easy for people and for machines to use.
  • Keep facts consistent. Names, indications and safety wording should match across your pages and your listings.
  • Cite your sources on the page. Pages that show where each statement came from are easier to trust.
  • Check what AI tools say. Ask them the questions your audiences ask. Record any wrong or unsafe answer, and fix the source pages first.
  • Know the limits. No method guarantees that an AI tool will cite you, and regulatory rules still apply to your own pages.

How long does pharma SEO take?

Google says some changes show in hours and others take months, and it suggests waiting a few weeks before judging a change. Pharma adds approval time before anything goes live. Plan for six to twelve months before you judge the program, and for a few months before the first pages are live.

A 90-day plan to start

DaysWorkOutput
1 to 14Audit indexing, page ownership and technical health; list audiences and marketsStarting point and a fix list
15 to 30Build the keyword map; agree page designs and approved language with the review teamMap and page models agreed once
31 to 60Fix the technical basics; write and submit the first three to five pages for reviewPages in approval
61 to 90Publish approved pages; set up measurement; test AI answers for your key questionsFirst pages live and a monthly report

Should you hire a pharmaceutical SEO company?

Some teams run SEO in-house with medical writers and a technical lead. Others use an agency for strategy, technical work and reporting. Whichever you choose, the same questions apply. Ask any pharmaceutical SEO company or agency:

  • Which audiences and markets have you worked in, and which rules do you plan around?
  • How will you work with our medical, legal and regulatory team, and when does SEO enter the process?
  • Who writes and who reviews the content, and what are their qualifications?
  • How do you report results, and can you tie them to enquiries or other business goals?
  • How do you earn links? Google lists buying links to affect rankings as link spam.
  • How do you check AI answers about our products?
  • What is in the written scope, and how can we end the contract?

Be careful with anyone who promises a ranking date or guarantees approvals. Nobody controls Google, and your own regulatory team controls approvals. Reinforce Lab also offers search services to pharmaceutical companies, so read this guide with that in mind. It was written by a team whose founder trained as a pharmacist and worked in pharmaceutical marketing.

Common pharma SEO mistakes

  • Adding SEO after review. A small change then triggers a new approval round.
  • Mixing audiences. One keyword list for patients, professionals and buyers makes pages that serve none.
  • Gating the wrong pages. If professional content is the landing page, public searchers find nothing to read.
  • Writing benefit-led titles. A title or description can carry a claim.
  • Linking education straight to promotion. Ask your regulatory team first.
  • No author, reviewer or date. Health pages without them lose trust.
  • Copying competitor pages. Duplicate pages do not earn authority.
  • Letting facts drift. Out-of-date doses and indications are a risk for patients and for you.
  • Buying links. Short-term gain, long-term risk.

A quick checklist

  • One page owner for each target search
  • Audiences and markets listed, each page tied to one
  • Keyword map with a reviewer for every page
  • Page designs and approved wording agreed before drafting
  • Author, reviewer, sources and dates visible on every health page
  • Professional-only content clearly marked, and public pages indexable
  • Titles and descriptions checked for claims
  • Technical basics fixed and measured
  • AI answers about your key questions checked each quarter
  • Monthly report that ties search to business goals

Final thoughts

Pharma SEO works when search and regulatory teams plan together from the start. Pick the audience, name the page that owns each search, show evidence a reader can check and measure in stages. The first few pages take longest. After that, the approved models make every new page faster to publish and safer to maintain.
